records.name: Niger
records.summary:
Niger State operates Sharia criminal law as part of the twelve-state northern bloc adopted by 2002, with Sharia courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslim defendants (Human Rights Watch, 2004). The federal anti-discrimination statute criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide; the UK Home Office country note (June 2025) records that the Sharia layer in these states extends criminalisation to acts between women.

No Kebbi-style state-specific enforcement or Hisbah record against trans people is documented for Niger; case-level enforcement records exist for other bloc states. The Sharia system adds a parallel criminal jurisdiction that the federation's southern states do not have, under which an outed Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor faces broader charges and harsher penalties than under federal law alone.

records.name: Edo
records.summary:
In May 2018 in Ekpoma, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. The coverage framed the act as an 'abominable' one defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land', and no prosecution is recorded: customary moral judgement operating lethally, with complete impunity. For national context, a rights-monitoring report published in January 2025 documented 556 violations against real or perceived LGBT people affecting 850 victims across Nigeria in 2024 — and states these are only a fraction of the true scale.

Edo's finding is the Ekpoma killing itself: where a discovered visitor can face lethal 'community justice' invoked in the name of tradition, answered afterwards by nobody.

records.name: Central Kalimantan
records.summary:
Central Kalimantan is listed in the dossier among the provinces with no sub-national signal: no enacted discriminatory bylaw, raid, arrest or incident series targeting transgender people was found, and the province is NOT one of the eight identified in OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation analysis of discriminatory regional regulations (that list covers Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta).

For a visitor, Central Kalimantan therefore tracks the national baseline: the KUHP criminal code in force from 1 January 2026 criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide, and ordinary Sumatran/Java-style local moral policing is absent here — but there is no province-specific enforcement record in either direction. Any risk follows the country's national framework rather than a local divergence.
